source: Oh, my. With pirates at our throats and imminent death on the horizon, I'm really clinching a new girlfriend at the last minute, aren't I?
Oh, my. With the political situation crumbling and imminent death on the horizon, I'm really clinching a new girlfriend at the last minute, aren't I?
Um, speaking of which...
I'd rather we were just friends. But that doesn't mean I don't like you.
All right! You know, you're the first good friend I've had since Hamlet and Rosie came along.
If the pirates decide to cannibalize our flesh after all, as I suspect they might, I hope you find someone who makes you feel happy all the time.
If Norway sweeps in and murders us all, as I have an inexplicable inkling they might, I hope you find someone who makes you feel happy all the time.
Rosie makes me feel that way. And you do, too.
You even helped me plan a fake funeral. If that's not friendship, what is?
You deserve something like that.
Oh, I'm certain we'll meet again. No matter what happens.
Can you keep a secret?
Well, I suppose it doesn't matter much either way.
I have something to tell you.
Are you a spy? I knew it!
No. But I've been experiencing something most curious.
For me, time is repeating itself. I've seen the ebb and flow of Elsinore castle, but—changed.
And I'm trying to change that outcome. To reach a better place for us all.
And I've been trying to change our collective dismal future for a long time now.
Oh! I see. Like a time loop!
You believe me?
I've-- I've actually been here with you before.
Well, not in this precise moment. But something quite similar.
It's still surprising you believe me so easily.
Of course. Rosie and I travel everywhere. We've seen all sorts of strange things. Like a Danish boy named Hamlet, for example. What a ridiculous name.
It sounds like the kind of thing you'd put in a room to decorate a corner. 'Oh, and here's an antique vase, next to that Hamlet over there. Brightens up the room.'
Although I wouldn't have believed you if I hadn't gotten to know you like this. You do have a reputation as a bit of a loon.
Even if you were to die tomorrow, we'll see each other again. That's what I mean by all this.
That's wonderful.
Well, if I do die, then I hope the Guilda you meet in the next world is a good one.
And I hope you can find a way to help her be just as happy as I am now.
I'll do my absolute best. I promise.
Good. Then let's enjoy the nighttime stillness while we can.
I've only a moment. I must make haste.
What were they doing in here earlier, so secretive?
A letter from Claudius?
It bears the Seal of Denmark. Luckily, I've one of my own to match.
I've entrusted these orders to two loyal servants, Rosencrantz and Guildenstern, to ensure that...
He is to be executed upon arrival. He's asking for my death. The Queen of England is to remove my head.
Rosie and Guilda. They must know about this.
I knew they were under Claudius's thumb, but this is too far.
Were they ever my friends at all? Was anything they said to me about our camraderie ever true?
And of course, Claudius never had any intention of letting me live free in England. Ought to have seen that one coming.
I've made a fool of myself. And now the murderer rules Denmark free of anyone who knows his secret.
Ahh. Aren't you excited for our big return to England?
It's been such a long time since we ate and gallivanted our way around London!
A chance at something new.
You seem unhappy.
Merely cautious.
I'd prefer to be on solid ground in England, away from my uncle's clutches.
Listen, Guildenstern.
It's been good to see you both again. But once we set foot on land, I think we should depart one another's company.
For a long while, if not forever.
I'm well aware you were working with my uncle to watch over me. I don't like that.
Merely to observe, Hamlet. Everything we told you was the absolute truth.
They're worried about you, your mother and father. This—our voyage—it's all they can think to do.
So you see me as a menace, then.
I don't. And you know I never have!
Initially, I persuaded Rosie to come to Elsinore in part because... of what happened between us in Wittenberg.
I had assumed I would be part of your future.
I believe you were mistaken.
I apologize for not being clearer with my intentions.
Perhaps even for a short time back then I did love you. But things are different now.
I see. My feelings changed, too. I met someone. She's indescribably wonderful.
Well that's not something I expected to hear.
I'm not certain how she feels. But you know, I think I understand now why you could never love me over her.
In that moment, I forgave you. I forgave you for hurting me.
Then perhaps it's even better we parted ways in England. I can't reconcile your confession with the way I feel.
For years I have had trouble feeling strongly for anything, Guilda.
And now I feel strongly about this. Even if Ophelia doesn't return my affections, I love her still.
You don't love her. You love the idea of Ophelia.
Rosie warned me about you when we all first met. She said you were the type to bed foreign women. That we should stay away.
I was hoping that—when we arrived in England—we might discuss the future.
I had assumed I might be a part of that future for you.
Everything that happened between us in Wittenberg seemed...
I thought you had come to feel for me the way I had you.
Oh, no, don't tell me. I already know the answer. It's her, isn't it.
You certainly felt strongly enough about me to bed me.
Rosie warned me about you. She said you were the type to bed foreign women. That we should stay away.
That's it, isn't it? And that's why you'd do anything to be with Ophelia, too.
You can't simplify my feelings that way!
Oh, but it's true, isn't it?
We're like little items for you to collect! To build out your harem!
Before me, it was Emine, and others like her. Don't think I've forgotten.
I can see this concerns me, so I've come to insert myself.
You've heard what I said, then. I stand by it all the same.
What Guilda says is the truth, Hamlet. I've noticed it myself.
T-that's not true. My feelings for you have always been—complex.
And the others?
Have you ever loved another Danish woman?
I mean a true-blooded Dane, Hamlet. Not like me. Not someone foreign-born.
I don't see what that has to do with anything.
All men prefer a certain kind of beauty which is amenable to their tastes.
So do I. What have I done wrong to find women like the two of you attractive?
What does it matter if I've never loved anyone who looks like Brit?
I find that sort of woman to be tiresome anyway.
I don't think he realizes.
Hamlet. Think upon it a moment. What did you mean when you said you found that sort of woman to be tiresome?
Women like 'her.' The lily-faced, fair-haired sort who loudly protest every whim. And Danish women who look like her are all that way.
Merely being near women like that is exhausting. I far prefer the company of women of your nature. You know. real women.
And so--you feel that 'all women' like myself and Lady Guildenstern are somehow—different?
Of course. Isn't that clear? You sort are far kindlier, with greater cheer and a captivating graciousness.
Graciousness? Is that what you call it?
At Wittenberg, women who looked like Ophelia and me were afraid to refuse you. You're a Prince.
And if one of us was to spurn your advances, and you were to become angry for it? Well, then.
I would never begrudge a woman for something like that!
Oh, never? Come now, Hamlet.
Do not mistake fear for graciousness, Hamlet. Or you're more the fool than I ever thought.
We may be landed, styled women, but we are not equal to you. Not in this world. Not in Denmark.
And you used that against us to find your next match.
What she says is the truth. It is the reason I told you never to speak to me again.
It is all too easy for you to ruin us.
And we know this. It is only you who remain blind to it.
Clearly I've made a great number of women uncomfortable.
Am I truly so blind to this element of the world, then?
You're both right. I have this power, whether I ever wanted it or not. And I was too absorbed within myself to see it.
Please excuse me. We may be friends still, but I find a sudden pressing urge to flee you.
Ugh. Ophelia, what have I done?
Don't look to me for answers or comfort. You'll find your own way. You always seem to.
I am a fool.
Trustworthiness aside, what Guilda said...
It wasn't wrong.
The way I think about her, and Ophelia...
I didn't think there was anything amiss with it, until now.
But how many women have I hurt?
Am I just some irredeemable monster?
Everyone despises me. All I do is cause pain.
I don't know how to fix it. Or how to be better.
But starting today, I have to be better.
So long as I choose to live, I choose to better myself.
C-Captain, we're under attack!
Stations, men. Hold firm.
Under attack? No, friends. You've already lost.
How did she—?
Came 'round yer flank. You were all lookin' at the cannons of my ship, weren't you?
Anyhow, be on yer knees and relinquish yer cargo, and nobody has to lose a limb.
Cease at once! Don't you know who this ship belongs to?
Well, the Danish emblem on th'sails gives me a wee inkling...
He won't let you take her over so easily. Will you, Hamlet?
Ah... Guildenstern...
Well, well. 'Hamlet'! Yer the most English-soundin' Dane I've ever met in all m'years. That wouldn't be Prince Hamlet, would it?
Yes. I am Prince Hamlet. And on behalf of my people aboard this ship, I order you to stand down at once, or risk immediate war with my country.
After three seconds o' deliberation, my answer is 'no.' However, I'll happily take you as a hostage for ransom.
Hamlet. We're outnumbered. There's no sense in anyone losing their life.
Go with them. Do what they say.
No. I can't leave you, Ophelia.
Sweet on the Moor, eh?
I won't abandon her. She's here by my sake. And I won't leave her behind. So kill me if you must. I'll not go, nor deliver her into the hands of thieves.
